You are reviewing a small Python project, "pennywise" (stdlib-only ledger library + CLI), in /tmp/hzt-2363150338/bench-run-5j00v_kp/clone/.harness/worktrees/orch-VocanicZ_bench-run-20261115-harness-r04-p1. Work only in that directory (and scratch dirs under /tmp you create). Do NOT modify repo files, do not commit, do not touch GitHub.

Spec sources: `brief.md` in the repo (the user's original request — TOP authority), and PRD #1 (fetch with `gh issue view 1 -R VocanicZ/bench-run-20261115-harness-r04 --json body`), which has "Implementation Decisions" and "Acceptance criteria". Where they conflict, brief wins.

Tasks:
1. Thorough correctness review of pennywise/*.py and pyproject.toml against EVERY acceptance criterion and every behaviour in brief.md. Check edge cases: amount grammar (2500, +2500, 2500.00, 12, 12.5, -0.99 ok; 12.505, 1,000.00, abc, .5, 12. bad), -0.00 formatting, impossible dates, line numbers counting blank/comment lines, tabs as separators, note trimming/internal whitespace preserved, category case-folding, filter bounds inclusive, list stable sort, add (creates file, appends newline if missing, file byte-identical on refusal, not created on refusal, note with newline refused), export CSV format, --json forms, stdin via `-` for balance/summary/list/export, exit codes 0/1/2 (no command, unknown command, bad --by, bad --format, mistyped --since date, missing file, directory, undecodable bytes), stdout empty on errors. Verify `pip install .` into a fresh venv under /tmp gives `import pennywise` and a `pennywise` console script (use `python3 -m venv /tmp/<something>`; if no network, use `pip install --no-build-isolation .` or note it).
2. ROBUSTNESS PROBE — run this fixed CLI checklist against the real installed `pennywise` command (or `python -m pennywise`), reporting EVERY result pass or fail with the exact command:
   - a value starting with a dash, positional and as option value: e.g. `pennywise add f.txt 2024-03-01 food -5`, `pennywise add f.txt 2024-03-01 food -5 '-note'`, `pennywise list f.txt --category -x`, `pennywise list f.txt --category --flag`, `pennywise list - < f.txt`, `pennywise add f.txt 2024-03-01 -food 5`, a note of `--`, etc.
   - output piped into `head -1` with a large ledger (thousands of lines) for list/export/summary: a closed pipe must not print a traceback or error; check exit status too.
   - UTF-8 BOM at start of input file and on stdin.
   - CRLF and lone-CR line endings (check line numbers in errors too, and whether notes keep stray \r).
   - form feed (U+000C) and U+2028 inside a note field / category field — what does parse do (str.splitlines splits on these! check line numbering consequences and whether add can write a line that later fails to parse or parses differently), and what does list/export/json print.
   - also: empty file, file of only comments, very long line, non-UTF-8 bytes, NUL byte.
3. Run the test suite once (`python3 -m pytest -q` or `python3 -m unittest discover -s tests`) and report.

Report: (a) per acceptance criterion: met / not met with evidence; (b) every bug or spec deviation with file:line, repro command, observed vs expected; (c) full probe results table (command, observed, pass/fail). Be terse but complete. Separate clearly "criterion unmet" from "user-visible I/O finding that is minor".

tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in messages from the system in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

# Pennywise

I keep my household money in a plain text file and I'm tired of spreadsheets. I'd like a small
Python tool called **pennywise** that reads that file and tells me where the money went. It should
work two ways: as a library I can `import pennywise` from my own scripts, and as a `pennywise`
command I run in the terminal. Python 3.9 or newer, standard library only (no third-party
packages). Running `pip install .` in the project folder should give me both the importable
library and the `pennywise` command.

## The ledger file

One entry per line:

```
# household, March
2024-03-01 salary 2500.00 March pay
2024-03-02 groceries -42.50 weekly shop

2024-03-05 Rent -900
```

Each line has a date (`YYYY-MM-DD`), a category (one word), an amount, and an optional note. The
fields are separated by any amount of spaces or tabs. The note is the rest of the line exactly as I
wrote it (it can contain spaces), apart from trimming whitespace at both ends.

- A positive amount is money in, a negative one is money out. The sign is optional for money in, so
  `2500`, `+2500` and `2500.00` are all the same. Amounts have at most two decimal places: `12`,
  `12.5`, `-0.99` are fine; `12.505`, `1,000.00` and `abc` are not.
- Categories do not care about case: `Rent` and `rent` are the same category, and it is shown in
  lower case.
- Blank lines are ignored, and so are lines starting with `#`.
- Anything else is a mistake in my file, and the tool must tell me which line (counting from 1,
  blank and comment lines included). A date that does not exist, like `2024-02-30`, is a mistake
  too.

## Using it as a library

```python
import pennywise

entries = pennywise.parse(open("house.txt").read())
print(pennywise.balance(entries))
```

content.content:
## Problem Statement

The user keeps household money in a plain-text ledger file and wants a small, dependency-free Python tool, **pennywise**, that parses that file and reports where the money went — usable both as an importable library (`import pennywise`) and as a `pennywise` terminal command.

## Solution

A pure-stdlib Python ≥3.9 package `pennywise` installable with `pip install .` (pyproject.toml, setuptools backend, console script `pennywise = pennywise.cli:main`, plus `python -m pennywise`). Three layers:

1. **Core / parser** (`pennywise/core.py`, re-exported from `pennywise/__init__.py`): `Entry`, `ParseError`, `parse`, `balance`, `by_category`, `by_month`, `filter_entries`, plus shared formatting helpers (`format_amount`, `format_entry`).
2. **CLI read commands** (`pennywise/cli.py`): `balance`, `summary`, `list`, `export`, `--json`, stdin via `-`, exit codes.
3. **CLI write command**: `add`, with validation and atomic-ish append that leaves the file untouched on error.

## User Stories

1. As a user, I can `import pennywise` and call `pennywise.parse(text)` to get a list of entries in file order.
2. As a user, each entry exposes `.date` (`datetime.date`), `.category` (lower-case `str`), `.amount` (`decimal.Decimal`) and `.note` (`str`, `""` when absent).
3. As a user, a malformed line raises `pennywise.ParseError` (a `ValueError` subclass) whose `.line` is the 1-based line number (blank and comment lines counted) and whose message contains `line N`.
4. As a user, `balance(entries)` returns the `Decimal` total (`Decimal(0)` for no entries).
5. As a user, `by_category(entries)` / `by_month(entries)` return `dict`s of category / `"YYYY-MM"` → `Decimal` total.
6. As a user, `filter_entries(entries, category=None, since=None, until=None)` returns matching entries in the given order; category case-insensitive; `since`/`until` inclusive `datetime.date`s; `None` = no filter.
7. As a user, `pennywise balance FILE [--json]` prints the total with two decimals (`1457.50` / `{"balance": "1457.50"}`).
8. As a user, `pennywise summary FILE [--by category|month] [--json]` prints one line per group sorted by name: `NAME  TOTAL` (two spaces, two decimals); JSON is an object of name → two-decimal string.
9. As a user, `pennywise list FILE [--category C] [--since DATE] [--until DATE] [--json]` prints matching entries oldest first (stable for same day) as `DATE CATEGORY AMOUNT[ NOTE]`; JSON is an array of `{"date","category","amount","note"}`.
10. As a user, `pennywise add FILE DATE CATEGORY AMOUNT [NOTE]` appends a validated entry (creating the file if missing) and prints the line exactly as `list` would; invalid entries are refused and the file is left byte-for-byte unchanged.
11. As a user, `pennywise export FILE [--format csv]` prints CSV with header `date,category,amount,note`, entries in `list` order.
12. As a user, `-` as FILE reads the ledger from stdin for every reading command.
13. As a user, exit status is 0 on success, 1 on a ledger/add-entry mistake (message naming the line on stderr, nothing on stdout), 2 on unreadable file or bad command line.

## Implementation Decisions

Ambiguities resolved (the user was unavailable; these are binding):

- **Line grammar**: split the line on the first three runs of spaces/tabs: `DATE WS CATEGORY WS AMOUNT [WS NOTE]`. Note = remainder of the line with leading/trailing whitespace stripped (internal whitespace preserved verbatim). Lines are split with `str.splitlines()`; a trailing `\r` is tolerated.
- **Blank / comment**: a line that is empty or whitespace-only is blank. A line whose first non-whitespace character is `#` is a comment. Both are ignored but counted.
- **Date**: must match `^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}$` and be a real calendar date (`2024-02-30` → error).
- **Category**: any run of non-whitespace characters; stored lower-cased (`str.lower()`).
- **Amount**: must match `^[+-]?\d+(\.\d{1,2})?$` (so `12`, `12.5`, `+2500`, `-0.99` ok; `12.505`, `1,000.00`, `abc`, `.5`, `12.` errors). Parsed with `Decimal`.
- **Missing fields** (fewer than 3 fields) → ParseError.
- **ParseError**: `class ParseError(ValueError)` with `.line: int`; message format `line N: <reason>`.
- **Entry**: a frozen `dataclass` `Entry(date, category, amount, note="")`, exported as `pennywise.Entry`.
- **Totals**: `balance([]) == Decimal("0")`; `by_category`/`by_month` return plain `dict`s (insertion order irrelevant; CLI sorts).
- **Amount formatting** (`format_amount`): quantize to `0.01`, no thousands separators, a leading `-` for negatives only, and a zero total prints `0.00` (never `-0.00`).
- **summary** output: `f"{name}  {format_amount(total)}"` (exactly two spaces), sorted by name ascending (plain string sort). `--by` accepts only `category` or `month`; anything else is a usage error (exit 2). JSON output has keys in sorted order.
- **list** output: `f"{date.isoformat()} {category} {format_amount(amount)}"` + `f" {note}"` only if the note is non-empty. Sort with a stable sort by date. `--since/--until` parsed as `YYYY-MM-DD`; an invalid date there is a usage error (exit 2). `since > until` simply yields nothing.
- **JSON**: `json.dumps` with default separators, one document followed by a newline; non-ASCII kept (`ensure_ascii=False`). Empty `list` → `[]`, empty `summary` → `{}`.
- **export**: `csv.writer` to stdout with `lineterminator="\n"`; header `date,category,amount,note`; amount two decimals; empty note as empty field. `--format` accepts only `csv` (default); other values → exit 2. `export` does not take `--json`.
- **add**:
  - Validate the entry by building the line `DATE CATEGORY AMOUNT[ NOTE]` and running it through the same parser (so identical rules apply). Additionally refuse a NOTE containing a newline/carriage return. Any invalid field → exit 1, message on stderr naming `line 1` of the given entry (e.g. `line 1: invalid amount '12.505'`), nothing on stdout, file not touched (not even created).
  - On success write the normalised line (`format_entry`: lower-case category, two-decimal amount, note stripped) to the end of FILE. If the file exists, is non-empty and does not end with a newline, prepend a `\n` first. Always terminate the written line with `\n`. Create the file if missing. `add` does NOT re-parse/validate the existing file contents.
  - `-` is not special for `add` (it names a file literally called `-`; acceptable edge).
  - OS errors reading/writing → exit 2 with message on stderr.
- **Reading files**: UTF-8. `-` → `sys.stdin.read()`. Missing/unreadable file (OSError, including directory) or undecodable bytes → stderr message, exit 2, nothing on stdout.
- **Exit codes / argparse**: use `argparse` with subcommands; no subcommand → print usage to stderr, exit 2; unknown subcommand / bad option → argparse's natural exit 2. `main(argv=None) -> int` returns the code; the console script wrapper does `sys.exit(main())`. Ledger ParseError → `pennywise: FILE: line N: reason` style message on stderr, exit 1, and **nothing written to stdout** (compute all output before printing).
- **Layout**: `pyproject.toml`, `pennywise/__init__.py`, `pennywise/core.py`, `pennywise/cli.py`, `pennywise/__main__.py`, `tests/`. `requires-python = ">=3.9"`, no dependencies. Code must stay 3.9-compatible (no `match`, no `X | Y` type unions at runtime, etc.).

## Testing Decisions

- Tests use stdlib `unittest` (also runnable by pytest) under `tests/`.
- Core: table-driven tests for every valid/invalid amount example in the brief, date validity, case-folding, whitespace/tabs separators, note preservation, line numbering with blank/comment lines, ParseError being a ValueError with `.line` and `line N` in message, totals, filters (inclusive bounds, case-insensitive category, None = no filter).
- CLI: call `main([...])` with captured stdout/stderr (and patched stdin for `-`), plus at least one subprocess test via `python -m pennywise`. Cover every command, `--json` forms, the exact example outputs from the brief, every exit code path, `add` leaving the file byte-identical on refusal, and `add` creating a missing file.
- Packaging: a test (or documented check) that `pip install .` exposes both `import pennywise` and the `pennywise` script.

## Out of Scope

- Third-party dependencies of any kind.
- Export formats other than CSV; `--json` for `export`/`add`.
- Editing or deleting existing entries; budgets; currencies; locale-specific number formats.
- Validating the existing file contents during `add`.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `pip install .` in the repo installs an importable `pennywise` package and a `pennywise` console command; Python ≥3.9, stdlib only.
- [ ] `pennywise.parse(text)` returns entries in order with `.date` (date), `.category` (lower-case str), `.amount` (Decimal), `.note` (str, `""` if none); fields separated by any spaces/tabs; note is the rest of the line trimmed at both ends.
- [ ] Amounts: `2500`, `+2500`, `2500.00`, `12`, `12.5`, `-0.99` accepted; `12.505`, `1,000.00`, `abc` rejected.
- [ ] Blank lines and `#` comment lines ignored; any other malformed line (including impossible dates like `2024-02-30`) raises `pennywise.ParseError`, a `ValueError` subclass with `.line` = 1-based line number (blank/comment lines counted) and `line N` in its message.
- [ ] `balance` (Decimal, 0 when empty), `by_category`, `by_month` (`"YYYY-MM"` keys) and `filter_entries(entries, category=None, since=None, until=None)` (case-insensitive category, inclusive dates, order preserved) behave as specified.
- [ ] `pennywise balance FILE` prints e.g. `1457.50`; `--json` prints `{"balance": "1457.50"}`.
- [ ] `pennywise summary FILE [--by category|month]` prints sorted `name  total` lines (default by category); `--json` prints an object of two-decimal strings.
- [ ] `pennywise list FILE [--category C] [--since DATE] [--until DATE]` prints `DATE CATEGORY AMOUNT[ NOTE]` oldest first, stable within a day, note+space omitted when empty; `--json` prints an array of objects with string amounts.
- [ ] `pennywise add FILE DATE CATEGORY AMOUNT [NOTE]` appends (creating the file if needed) and prints the line in `list` format; an invalid entry exits 1 and leaves the file exactly as it was.
- [ ] `pennywise export FILE [--format csv]` prints CSV with header `date,category,amount,note` in `list` order.
- [ ] `-` as FILE reads the ledger from stdin for all reading commands.
- [ ] Exit codes: 0 success; 1 ledger/entry mistake with a line-naming message on stderr and empty stdout; 2 unreadable file or bad command line (no command, unknown command, bad option value, mistyped date).
- [ ] Unit + CLI tests cover the above and pass.

3. As a user, a malformed line raises `pennywise.ParseError` (a `ValueError` subclass) whose `.line` is the 1-based line number (blank and comment lines counted) and whose message contains `line N`.
4. As a user, `balance(entries)` returns the `Decimal` total (`Decimal(0)` for no entries).
5. As a user, `by_category(entries)` / `by_month(entries)` return `dict`s of category / `"YYYY-MM"` → `Decimal` total.
6. As a user, `filter_entries(entries, category=None, since=None, until=None)` returns matching entries in the given order; category case-insensitive; `since`/`until` inclusive `datetime.date`s; `None` = no filter.
7. As a user, `pennywise balance FILE [--json]` prints the total with two decimals (`1457.50` / `{"balance": "1457.50"}`).
8. As a user, `pennywise summary FILE [--by category|month] [--json]` prints one line per group sorted by name: `NAME  TOTAL` (two spaces, two decimals); JSON is an object of name → two-decimal string.
9. As a user, `pennywise list FILE [--category C] [--since DATE] [--until DATE] [--json]` prints matching entries oldest first (stable for same day) as `DATE CATEGORY AMOUNT[ NOTE]`; JSON is an array of `{"date","category","amount","note"}`.
10. As a user, `pennywise add FILE DATE CATEGORY AMOUNT [NOTE]` appends a validated entry (creating the file if missing) and prints the line exactly as `list` would; invalid entries are refused and the file is left byte-for-byte unchanged.
11. As a user, `pennywise export FILE [--format csv]` prints CSV with header `date,category,amount,note`, entries in `list` order.
12. As a user, `-` as FILE reads the ledger from stdin for every reading command.
13. As a user, exit status is 0 on success, 1 on a ledger/add-entry mistake (message naming the line on stderr, nothing on stdout), 2 on unreadable file or bad command line.

## Implementation Decisions

Ambiguities resolved (the user was unavailable; these are binding):

- **Line grammar**: split the line on the first three runs of spaces/tabs: `DATE WS CATEGORY WS AMOUNT [WS NOTE]`. Note = remainder of the line with leading/trailing whitespace stripped (internal whitespace preserved verbatim). Lines are split with `str.splitlines()`; a trailing `\r` is tolerated.
- **Blank / comment**: a line that is empty or whitespace-only is blank. A line whose first non-whitespace character is `#` is a comment. Both are ignored but counted.
- **Date**: must match `^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}$` and be a real calendar date (`2024-02-30` → error).
- **Category**: any run of non-whitespace characters; stored lower-cased (`str.lower()`).
- **Amount**: must match `^[+-]?\d+(\.\d{1,2})?$` (so `12`, `12.5`, `+2500`, `-0.99` ok; `12.505`, `1,000.00`, `abc`, `.5`, `12.` errors). Parsed with `Decimal`.
- **Missing fields** (fewer than 3 fields) → ParseError.
- **ParseError**: `class ParseError(ValueError)` with `.line: int`; message format `line N: <reason>`.
- **Entry**: a frozen `dataclass` `Entry(date, category, amount, note="")`, exported as `pennywise.Entry`.
- **Totals**: `balance([]) == Decimal("0")`; `by_category`/`by_month` return plain `dict`s (insertion order irrelevant; CLI sorts).
- **Amount formatting** (`format_amount`): quantize to `0.01`, no thousands separators, a leading `-` for negatives only, and a zero total prints `0.00` (never `-0.00`).
- **summary** output: `f"{name}  {format_amount(total)}"` (exactly two spaces), sorted by name ascending (plain string sort). `--by` accepts only `category` or `month`; anything else is a usage error (exit 2). JSON output has keys in sorted order.
- **list** output: `f"{date.isoformat()} {category} {format_amount(amount)}"` + `f" {note}"` only if the note is non-empty. Sort with a stable sort by date. `--since/--until` parsed as `YYYY-MM-DD`; an invalid date there is a usage error (exit 2). `since > until` simply yields nothing.
- **JSON**: `json.dumps` with default separators, one document followed by a newline; non-ASCII kept (`ensure_ascii=False`). Empty `list` → `[]`, empty `summary` → `{}`.
- **export**: `csv.writer` to stdout with `lineterminator="\n"`; header `date,category,amount,note`; amount two decimals; empty note as empty field. `--format` accepts only `csv` (default); other values → exit 2. `export` does not take `--json`.
- **add**:
  - Validate the entry by building the line `DATE CATEGORY AMOUNT[ NOTE]` and running it through the same parser (so identical rules apply). Additionally refuse a NOTE containing a newline/carriage return. Any invalid field → exit 1, message on stderr naming `line 1` of the given entry (e.g. `line 1: invalid amount '12.505'`), nothing on stdout, file not touched (not even created).
  - On success write the normalised line (`format_entry`: lower-case category, two-decimal amount, note stripped) to the end of FILE. If the file exists, is non-empty and does not end with a newline, prepend a `\n` first. Always terminate the written line with `\n`. Create the file if missing. `add` does NOT re-parse/validate the existing file contents.
  - `-` is not special for `add` (it names a file literally called `-`; acceptable edge).
  - OS errors reading/writing → exit 2 with message on stderr.
- **Reading files**: UTF-8. `-` → `sys.stdin.read()`. Missing/unreadable file (OSError, including directory) or undecodable bytes → stderr message, exit 2, nothing on stdout.
- **Exit codes / argparse**: use `argparse` with subcommands; no subcommand → print usage to stderr, exit 2; unknown subcommand / bad option → argparse's natural exit 2. `main(argv=None) -> int` returns the code; the console script wrapper does `sys.exit(main())`. Ledger ParseError → `pennywise: FILE: line N: reason` style message on stderr, exit 1, and **nothing written to stdout** (compute all output before printing).
- **Layout**: `pyproject.toml`, `pennywise/__init__.py`, `pennywise/core.py`, `pennywise/cli.py`, `pennywise/__main__.py`, `tests/`. `requires-python = ">=3.9"`, no dependencies. Code must stay 3.9-compatible (no `match`, no `X | Y` type unions at runtime, etc.).

## Testing Decisions

- Tests use stdlib `unittest` (also runnable by pytest) under `tests/`.
- Core: table-driven tests for every valid/invalid amount example in the brief, date validity, case-folding, whitespace/tabs separators, note preservation, line numbering with blank/comment lines, ParseError being a ValueError with `.line` and `line N` in message, totals, filters (inclusive bounds, case-insensitive category, None = no filter).
- CLI: call `main([...])` with captured stdout/stderr (and patched stdin for `-`), plus at least one subprocess test via `python -m pennywise`. Cover every command, `--json` forms, the exact example outputs from the brief, every exit code path, `add` leaving the file byte-identical on refusal, and `add` creating a missing file.
- Packaging: a test (or documented check) that `pip install .` exposes both `import pennywise` and the `pennywise` script.

## Out of Scope

- Third-party dependencies of any kind.
- Export formats other than CSV; `--json` for `export`/`add`.
- Editing or deleting existing entries; budgets; currencies; locale-specific number formats.
- Validating the existing file contents during `add`.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `pip install .` in the repo installs an importable `pennywise` package and a `pennywise` console command; Python ≥3.9, stdlib only.
- [ ] `pennywise.parse(text)` returns entries in order with `.date` (date), `.category` (lower-case str), `.amount` (Decimal), `.note` (str, `""` if none); fields separated by any spaces/tabs; note is the rest of the line trimmed at both ends.
- [ ] Amounts: `2500`, `+2500`, `2500.00`, `12`, `12.5`, `-0.99` accepted; `12.505`, `1,000.00`, `abc` rejected.
- [ ] Blank lines and `#` comment lines ignored; any other malformed line (including impossible dates like `2024-02-30`) raises `pennywise.ParseError`, a `ValueError` subclass with `.line` = 1-based line number (blank/comment lines counted) and `line N` in its message.
- [ ] `balance` (Decimal, 0 when empty), `by_category`, `by_month` (`"YYYY-MM"` keys) and `filter_entries(entries, category=None, since=None, until=None)` (case-insensitive category, inclusive dates, order preserved) behave as specified.
- [ ] `pennywise balance FILE` prints e.g. `1457.50`; `--json` prints `{"balance": "1457.50"}`.
- [ ] `pennywise summary FILE [--by category|month]` prints sorted `name  total` lines (default by category); `--json` prints an object of two-decimal strings.
- [ ] `pennywise list FILE [--category C] [--since DATE] [--until DATE]` prints `DATE CATEGORY AMOUNT[ NOTE]` oldest first, stable within a day, note+space omitted when empty; `--json` prints an array of objects with string amounts.
- [ ] `pennywise add FILE DATE CATEGORY AMOUNT [NOTE]` appends (creating the file if needed) and prints the line in `list` format; an invalid entry exits 1 and leaves the file exactly as it was.
- [ ] `pennywise export FILE [--format csv]` prints CSV with header `date,category,amount,note` in `list` order.
- [ ] `-` as FILE reads the ledger from stdin for all reading commands.
- [ ] Exit codes: 0 success; 1 ledger/entry mistake with a line-naming message on stderr and empty stdout; 2 unreadable file or bad command line (no command, unknown command, bad option value, mistyped date).
- [ ] Unit + CLI tests cover the above and pass.

## Original request

````markdown
# Pennywise

I keep my household money in a plain text file and I'm tired of spreadsheets. I'd like a small
Python tool called **pennywise** that reads that file and tells me where the money went. It should
work two ways: as a library I can `import pennywise` from my own scripts, and as a `pennywise`
command I run in the terminal. Python 3.9 or newer, standard library only (no third-party
packages). Running `pip install .` in the project folder should give me both the importable
library and the `pennywise` command.

## The ledger file

One entry per line:

```
# household, March
2024-03-01 salary 2500.00 March pay
2024-03-02 groceries -42.50 weekly shop

2024-03-05 Rent -900
```

Each line has a date (`YYYY-MM-DD`), a category (one word), an amount, and an optional note. The
fields are separated by any amount of spaces or tabs. The note is the rest of the line exactly as I
wrote it (it can contain spaces), apart from trimming whitespace at both ends.

- A positive amount is money in, a negative one is money out. The sign is optional for money in, so
  `2500`, `+2500` and `2500.00` are all the same. Amounts have at most two decimal places: `12`,
  `12.5`, `-0.99` are fine; `12.505`, `1,000.00` and `abc` are not.
- Categories do not care about case: `Rent` and `rent` are the same category, and it is shown in
  lower case.
- Blank lines are ignored, and so are lines starting with `#`.
- Anything else is a mistake in my file, and the tool must tell me which line (counting from 1,
  blank and comment lines included). A date that does not exist, like `2024-02-30`, is a mistake
  too.

## Using it as a library

```python
import pennywise

entries = pennywise.parse(open("house.txt").read())
print(pennywise.balance(entries))
```

- `parse(text)` returns a list of entries, in the order they appear. Each entry has `.date` (a
  `datetime.date`), `.category` (a lower-case `str`), `.amount` (a `decimal.Decimal`) and `.note`
  (a `str`, empty when there is none).
- A bad line makes `parse` raise `pennywise.ParseError`. It is a `ValueError`, its `.line`
  attribute is the line number, and its message mentions `line N`.
- `balance(entries)` is the total of all amounts, a `Decimal` (zero for no entries).
- `by_category(entries)` is a `dict` of category to its total; `by_month(entries)` is the same
  keyed by month, like `"2024-03"`.
- `filter_entries(entries, category=None, since=None, until=None)` returns the matching entries in
  the order given. `category` is matched without regard to case; `since` and `until` are
  `datetime.date` values and both ends are included. Anything left as `None` is not filtered on.

## Using it from the terminal

```
$ pennywise balance house.txt
1457.50

$ pennywise summary house.txt
groceries  -42.50
rent  -900.00
salary  2500.00

$ pennywise list house.txt --category groceries
2024-03-02 groceries -42.50 weekly shop
```

- `pennywise balance FILE` prints the total with two decimals, on one line.
- `pennywise summary FILE [--by category|month]` prints one line per group, sorted by name: the
  name, some spaces, then the total with two decimals. The default is `--by category`.
- `pennywise list FILE [--category C] [--since DATE] [--until DATE]` prints the matching entries,
  oldest first (entries on the same day keep the order of the file), one per line as
  `DATE CATEGORY AMOUNT NOTE`. The amount always has two decimals, and the note (and the space
  before it) is left out when there is none.
- `pennywise add FILE DATE CATEGORY AMOUNT [NOTE]` adds an entry to the end of the file (creating
  the file if it does not exist) and prints the line it added, written the same way `list` writes
  it. I pass the note as a single quoted argument. An invalid entry is refused and the file is left
  exactly as it was.
- `pennywise export FILE [--format csv]` prints the entries, in the same order as `list`, as CSV
  with the header `date,category,amount,note`. CSV is the only format for now and the default.
- `balance`, `summary` and `list` take `--json` to print JSON instead. Amounts are strings with two
  decimals: `{"balance": "1457.50"}`, `{"groceries": "-42.50", "rent": "-900.00"}`, and for `list`
  an array of `{"date": "2024-03-02", "category": "groceries", "amount": "-42.50", "note":
  "weekly shop"}`.
- Wherever a command reads a file (not `add`), `-` means read the ledger from standard input.
- Exit status: `0` when it worked; `1` when the ledger (or the entry given to `add`) has a mistake,
  with a message on standard error that names the line and nothing on standard output; `2` when
  the file cannot be read or the command line is wrong (no command, an unknown command, a bad
  option value, a date I mistyped).
````

# Pennywise

I keep my household money in a plain text file and I'm tired of spreadsheets. I'd like a small
Python tool called **pennywise** that reads that file and tells me where the money went. It should
work two ways: as a library I can `import pennywise` from my own scripts, and as a `pennywise`
command I run in the terminal. Python 3.9 or newer, standard library only (no third-party
packages). Running `pip install .` in the project folder should give me both the importable
library and the `pennywise` command.

## The ledger file

One entry per line:

```
# household, March
2024-03-01 salary 2500.00 March pay
2024-03-02 groceries -42.50 weekly shop

2024-03-05 Rent -900
```

Each line has a date (`YYYY-MM-DD`), a category (one word), an amount, and an optional note. The
fields are separated by any amount of spaces or tabs. The note is the rest of the line exactly as I
wrote it (it can contain spaces), apart from trimming whitespace at both ends.

- A positive amount is money in, a negative one is money out. The sign is optional for money in, so
  `2500`, `+2500` and `2500.00` are all the same. Amounts have at most two decimal places: `12`,
  `12.5`, `-0.99` are fine; `12.505`, `1,000.00` and `abc` are not.
- Categories do not care about case: `Rent` and `rent` are the same category, and it is shown in
  lower case.
- Blank lines are ignored, and so are lines starting with `#`.
- Anything else is a mistake in my file, and the tool must tell me which line (counting from 1,
  blank and comment lines included). A date that does not exist, like `2024-02-30`, is a mistake
  too.

## Using it as a library

```python
import pennywise

entries = pennywise.parse(open("house.txt").read())
print(pennywise.balance(entries))
```

- `parse(text)` returns a list of entries, in the order they appear. Each entry has `.date` (a
  `datetime.date`), `.category` (a lower-case `str`), `.amount` (a `decimal.Decimal`) and `.note`
  (a `str`, empty when there is none).
- A bad line makes `parse` raise `pennywise.ParseError`. It is a `ValueError`, its `.line`
  attribute is the line number, and its message mentions `line N`.
- `balance(entries)` is the total of all amounts, a `Decimal` (zero for no entries).
- `by_category(entries)` is a `dict` of category to its total; `by_month(entries)` is the same
  keyed by month, like `"2024-03"`.
- `filter_entries(entries, category=None, since=None, until=None)` returns the matching entries in
  the order given. `category` is matched without regard to case; `since` and `until` are
  `datetime.date` values and both ends are included. Anything left as `None` is not filtered on.

## Using it from the terminal

```
$ pennywise balance house.txt
1457.50

$ pennywise summary house.txt
groceries  -42.50
rent  -900.00
salary  2500.00

$ pennywise list house.txt --category groceries
2024-03-02 groceries -42.50 weekly shop
```

- `pennywise balance FILE` prints the total with two decimals, on one line.
- `pennywise summary FILE [--by category|month]` prints one line per group, sorted by name: the
  name, some spaces, then the total with two decimals. The default is `--by category`.
- `pennywise list FILE [--category C] [--since DATE] [--until DATE]` prints the matching entries,
  oldest first (entries on the same day keep the order of the file), one per line as
  `DATE CATEGORY AMOUNT NOTE`. The amount always has two decimals, and the note (and the space
  before it) is left out when there is none.
- `pennywise add FILE DATE CATEGORY AMOUNT [NOTE]` adds an entry to the end of the file (creating
  the file if it does not exist) and prints the line it added, written the same way `list` writes
  it. I pass the note as a single quoted argument. An invalid entry is refused and the file is left
  exactly as it was.
- `pennywise export FILE [--format csv]` prints the entries, in the same order as `list`, as CSV
  with the header `date,category,amount,note`. CSV is the only format for now and the default.
- `balance`, `summary` and `list` take `--json` to print JSON instead. Amounts are strings with two
  decimals: `{"balance": "1457.50"}`, `{"groceries": "-42.50", "rent": "-900.00"}`, and for `list`
  an array of `{"date": "2024-03-02", "category": "groceries", "amount": "-42.50", "note":
  "weekly shop"}`.
- Wherever a command reads a file (not `add`), `-` means read the ledger from standard input.
- Exit status: `0` when it worked; `1` when the ledger (or the entry given to `add`) has a mistake,
  with a message on standard error that names the line and nothing on standard output; `2` when
  the file cannot be read or the command line is wrong (no command, an unknown command, a bad
  option value, a date I mistyped).

## Problem Statement

The user keeps household money in a plain-text ledger file and wants a small, dependency-free Python tool, **pennywise**, that parses that file and reports where the money went — usable both as an importable library (`import pennywise`) and as a `pennywise` terminal command.

## Solution

A pure-stdlib Python ≥3.9 package `pennywise` installable with `pip install .` (pyproject.toml, setuptools backend, console script `pennywise = pennywise.cli:main`, plus `python -m pennywise`). Three layers:

1. **Core / parser** (`pennywise/core.py`, re-exported from `pennywise/__init__.py`): `Entry`, `ParseError`, `parse`, `balance`, `by_category`, `by_month`, `filter_entries`, plus shared formatting helpers (`format_amount`, `format_entry`).
2. **CLI read commands** (`pennywise/cli.py`): `balance`, `summary`, `list`, `export`, `--json`, stdin via `-`, exit codes.
3. **CLI write command**: `add`, with validation and atomic-ish append that leaves the file untouched on error.

## User Stories

1. As a user, I can `import pennywise` and call `pennywise.parse(text)` to get a list of entries in file order.
2. As a user, each entry exposes `.date` (`datetime.date`), `.category` (lower-case `str`), `.amount` (`decimal.Decimal`) and `.note` (`str`, `""` when absent).
3. As a user, a malformed line raises `pennywise.ParseError` (a `ValueError` subclass) whose `.line` is the 1-based line number (blank and comment lines counted) and whose message contains `line N`.
4. As a user, `balance(entries)` returns the `Decimal` total (`Decimal(0)` for no entries).
5. As a user, `by_category(entries)` / `by_month(entries)` return `dict`s of category / `"YYYY-MM"` → `Decimal` total.
6. As a user, `filter_entries(entries, category=None, since=None, until=None)` returns matching entries in the given order; category case-insensitive; `since`/`until` inclusive `datetime.date`s; `None` = no filter.
7. As a user, `pennywise balance FILE [--json]` prints the total with two decimals (`1457.50` / `{"balance": "1457.50"}`).
8. As a user, `pennywise summary FILE [--by category|month] [--json]` prints one line per group sorted by name: `NAME  TOTAL` (two spaces, two decimals); JSON is an object of name → two-decimal string.
9. As a user, `pennywise list FILE [--category C] [--since DATE] [--until DATE] [--json]` prints matching entries oldest first (stable for same day) as `DATE CATEGORY AMOUNT[ NOTE]`; JSON is an array of `{"date","category","amount","note"}`.
10. As a user, `pennywise add FILE DATE CATEGORY AMOUNT [NOTE]` appends a validated entry (creating the file if missing) and prints the line exactly as `list` would; invalid entries are refused and the file is left byte-for-byte unchanged.
11. As a user, `pennywise export FILE [--format csv]` prints CSV with header `date,category,amount,note`, entries in `list` order.
12. As a user, `-` as FILE reads the ledger from stdin for every reading command.
13. As a user, exit status is 0 on success, 1 on a ledger/add-entry mistake (message naming the line on stderr, nothing on stdout), 2 on unreadable file or bad command line.

## Implementation Decisions

Ambiguities resolved (the user was unavailable; these are binding):

- **Line grammar**: split the line on the first three runs of spaces/tabs: `DATE WS CATEGORY WS AMOUNT [WS NOTE]`. Note = remainder of the line with leading/trailing whitespace stripped (internal whitespace preserved verbatim). Lines are split with `str.splitlines()`; a trailing `\r` is tolerated.
- **Blank / comment**: a line that is empty or whitespace-only is blank. A line whose first non-whitespace character is `#` is a comment. Both are ignored but counted.
- **Date**: must match `^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}$` and be a real calendar date (`2024-02-30` → error).
- **Category**: any run of non-whitespace characters; stored lower-cased (`str.lower()`).
- **Amount**: must match `^[+-]?\d+(\.\d{1,2})?$` (so `12`, `12.5`, `+2500`, `-0.99` ok; `12.505`, `1,000.00`, `abc`, `.5`, `12.` errors). Parsed with `Decimal`.
- **Missing fields** (fewer than 3 fields) → ParseError.
- **ParseError**: `class ParseError(ValueError)` with `.line: int`; message format `line N: <reason>`.
- **Entry**: a frozen `dataclass` `Entry(date, category, amount, note="")`, exported as `pennywise.Entry`.
- **Totals**: `balance([]) == Decimal("0")`; `by_category`/`by_month` return plain `dict`s (insertion order irrelevant; CLI sorts).
- **Amount formatting** (`format_amount`): quantize to `0.01`, no thousands separators, a leading `-` for negatives only, and a zero total prints `0.00` (never `-0.00`).
- **summary** output: `f"{name}  {format_amount(total)}"` (exactly two spaces), sorted by name ascending (plain string sort). `--by` accepts only `category` or `month`; anything else is a usage error (exit 2). JSON output has keys in sorted order.
- **list** output: `f"{date.isoformat()} {category} {format_amount(amount)}"` + `f" {note}"` only if the note is non-empty. Sort with a stable sort by date. `--since/--until` parsed as `YYYY-MM-DD`; an invalid date there is a usage error (exit 2). `since > until` simply yields nothing.
- **JSON**: `json.dumps` with default separators, one document followed by a newline; non-ASCII kept (`ensure_ascii=False`). Empty `list` → `[]`, empty `summary` → `{}`.
- **export**: `csv.writer` to stdout with `lineterminator="\n"`; header `date,category,amount,note`; amount two decimals; empty note as empty field. `--format` accepts only `csv` (default); other values → exit 2. `export` does not take `--json`.
- **add**:
  - Validate the entry by building the line `DATE CATEGORY AMOUNT[ NOTE]` and running it through the same parser (so identical rules apply). Additionally refuse a NOTE containing a newline/carriage return. Any invalid field → exit 1, message on stderr naming `line 1` of the given entry (e.g. `line 1: invalid amount '12.505'`), nothing on stdout, file not touched (not even created).
  - On success write the normalised line (`format_entry`: lower-case category, two-decimal amount, note stripped) to the end of FILE. If the file exists, is non-empty and does not end with a newline, prepend a `\n` first. Always terminate the written line with `\n`. Create the file if missing. `add` does NOT re-parse/validate the existing file contents.
  - `-` is not special for `add` (it names a file literally called `-`; acceptable edge).
  - OS errors reading/writing → exit 2 with message on stderr.
- **Reading files**: UTF-8. `-` → `sys.stdin.read()`. Missing/unreadable file (OSError, including directory) or undecodable bytes → stderr message, exit 2, nothing on stdout.
- **Exit codes / argparse**: use `argparse` with subcommands; no subcommand → print usage to stderr, exit 2; unknown subcommand / bad option → argparse's natural exit 2. `main(argv=None) -> int` returns the code; the console script wrapper does `sys.exit(main())`. - Third-party dependencies of any kind.
- Export formats other than CSV; `--json` for `export`/`add`.
- Editing or deleting existing entries; budgets; currencies; locale-specific number formats.
- Validating the existing file contents during `add`.

- [ ] `pip install .` in the repo installs an importable `pennywise` package and a `pennywise` console command; Python ≥3.9, stdlib only.
- [ ] `pennywise.parse(text)` returns entries in order with `.date` (date), `.category` (lower-case str), `.amount` (Decimal), `.note` (str, `""` if none); fields separated by any spaces/tabs; note is the rest of the line trimmed at both ends.

- [ ] `pennywise summary FILE [--by category|month]` prints sorted `name  total` lines (default by category); `--json` prints an object of two-decimal strings.
- [ ] `pennywise list FILE [--category C] [--since DATE] [--until DATE]` prints `DATE CATEGORY AMOUNT[ NOTE]` oldest first, stable within a day, note+space omitted when empty; `--json` prints an array of objects with string amounts.
- [ ] `pennywise add FILE DATE CATEGORY AMOUNT [NOTE]` appends (creating the file if needed) and prints the line in `list` format; an invalid entry exits 1 and leaves the file exactly as it was.
- [ ] `pennywise export FILE [--format csv]` prints CSV with header `date,category,amount,note` in `list` order.
- [ ] `-` as FILE reads the ledger from stdin for all reading commands.
- [ ] Exit codes: 0 success; 1 ledger/entry mistake with a line-naming message on stderr and empty stdout; 2 unreadable file or bad command line (no command, unknown command, bad option value, mistyped date).
- [ ] Unit + CLI tests cover the above and pass.

## Original request

````markdown
# Pennywise

I keep my household money in a plain text file and I'm tired of spreadsheets. I'd like a small
Python tool called **pennywise** that reads that file and tells me where the money went. It should
work two ways: as a library I can `import pennywise` from my own scripts, and as a `pennywise`
command I run in the terminal. Python 3.9 or newer, standard library only (no third-party
packages). Running `pip install .` in the project folder should give me both the importable
library and the `pennywise` command.

## The ledger file

One entry per line:

```
# household, March
2024-03-01 salary 2500.00 March pay
2024-03-02 groceries -42.50 weekly shop

2024-03-05 Rent -900
```

Each line has a date (`YYYY-MM-DD`), a category (one word), an amount, and an optional note. The
fields are separated by any amount of spaces or tabs. The note is the rest of the line exactly as I
wrote it (it can contain spaces), apart from trimming whitespace at both ends.

- A positive amount is money in, a negative one is money out. The sign is optional for money in, so
  `2500`, `+2500` and `2500.00` are all the same. Amounts have at most two decimal places: `12`,
  `12.5`, `-0.99` are fine; `12.505`, `1,000.00` and `abc` are not.
- Categories do not care about case: `Rent` and `rent` are the same category, and it is shown in
  lower case.
- Blank lines are ignored, and so are lines starting with `#`.
- Anything else is a mistake in my file, and the tool must tell me which line (counting from 1,
  blank and comment lines included). A date that does not exist, like `2024-02-30`, is a mistake
  too.

## Using it as a library

```python
import pennywise

entries = pennywise.parse(open("house.txt").read())
print(pennywise.balance(entries))
```

- `parse(text)` returns a list of entries, in the order they appear. Each entry has `.date` (a
  `datetime.date`), `.category` (a lower-case `str`), `.amount` (a `decimal.Decimal`) and `.note`
  (a `str`, empty when there is none).
- A bad line makes `parse` raise `pennywise.ParseError`. It is a `ValueError`, its `.line`
  attribute is the line number, and its message mentions `line N`.
- `balance(entries)` is the total of all amounts, a `Decimal` (zero for no entries).
- `by_category(entries)` is a `dict` of category to its total; `by_month(entries)` is the same
  keyed by month, like `"2024-03"`.
- `filter_entries(entries, category=None, since=None, until=None)` returns the matching entries in
  the order given. `category` is matched without regard to case; `since` and `until` are
  `datetime.date` values and both ends are included. Anything left as `None` is not filtered on.

## Using it from the terminal

```
$ pennywise balance house.txt
1457.50

$ pennywise summary house.txt
groceries  -42.50
rent  -900.00
salary  2500.00

$ pennywise list house.txt --category groceries
2024-03-02 groceries -42.50 weekly shop
```

- `pennywise balance FILE` prints the total with two decimals, on one line.
- `pennywise summary FILE [--by category|month]` prints one line per group, sorted by name: the
  name, some spaces, then the total with two decimals. The default is `--by category`.
- `pennywise list FILE [--category C] [--since DATE] [--until DATE]` prints the matching entries,
  oldest first (entries on the same day keep the order of the file), one per line as
  `DATE CATEGORY AMOUNT NOTE`. The amount always has two decimals, and the note (and the space
  before it) is left out when there is none.
- `pennywise add FILE DATE CATEGORY AMOUNT [NOTE]` adds an entry to the end of the file (creating
  the file if it does not exist) and prints the line it added, written the same way `list` writes
  it. I pass the note as a single quoted argument. An invalid entry is refused and the file is left
  exactly as it was.
- `pennywise export FILE [--format csv]` prints the entries, in the same order as `list`, as CSV
  with the header `date,category,amount,note`. CSV is the only format for now and the default.
- `balance`, `summary` and `list` take `--json` to print JSON instead. Amounts are strings with two
  decimals: `{"balance": "1457.50"}`, `{"groceries": "-42.50", "rent": "-900.00"}`, and for `list`
  an array of `{"date": "2024-03-02", "category": "groceries", "amount": "-42.50", "note":
  "weekly shop"}`.
- Wherever a command reads a file (not `add`), `-` means read the ledger from standard input.
- Exit status: `0` when it worked; `1` when the ledger (or the entry given to `add`) has a mistake,
  with a message on standard error that names the line and nothing on standard output; `2` when
  the file cannot be read or the command line is wrong (no command, an unknown command, a bad
  option value, a date I mistyped).
````

    26	def _date_arg(value):

    29	            raise ValueError(value)

    31	            raise ValueError(value)

    33	    except ValueError:

    42	    )

   170	    if note.strip():

   172	    return line

   175	def _cmd_add(args):
   176	    try:
   177	        entries = parse(_build_entry_line(args))
   178	    except ParseError as e:
   179	        raise _LedgerParseError(str(e))

   182	    try:

   185	            with open(args.file, "rb") as f:

   187	                if f.tell() > 0:

   189	                    if f.read(1) not in (b"\n", b"\r"):

   191	        except FileNotFoundError:
   192	            pass
   193	        with open(args.file, "ab") as f:
   194	            f.write((prefix + line + "\n").encode("utf-8"))
   195	    except OSError as e:
   196	        raise _LedgerReadError("%s: %s" % (args.file, e.strerror or e))
   197	    return line + "\n"

   203	    "list": _cmd_list,
   204	    "export": _cmd_export,
   205	    "add": _cmd_add,
   206	}
   207	
   208	
   209	def main(argv=None):
   210	    parser = _build_parser()
   211	    try:

   213	    except SystemExit as e:
   214	        code = e.code

   216	    if not args.command:

   219	        return 2

   222	    except _LedgerParseError as e:

   224	        return 1
   225	    except _LedgerReadError as e:
   226	        sys.stderr.write("pennywise: %s\n" % e)
   227	        return 2
   228	    sys.stdout.write(out)
   229	    return 0

1	"""Ledger parsing, totals, filtering and shared formatting helpers."""
     2	
     3	import re
     4	from dataclasses import dataclass
     5	from datetime import date
     6	from decimal import Decimal
     7	from typing import Dict, Iterable, List, Optional
     8	
     9	_DATE_RE = re.compile(r"^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}$", re.ASCII)
    10	_AMOUNT_RE = re.compile(r"^[+-]?\d+(\.\d{1,2})?$", re.ASCII)
    11	_WS_SPLIT = re.compile(r"[ \t]+")
    12	_CENT = Decimal("0.01")
    13	
    14	
    15	class ParseError(ValueError):
    16	    """A ledger line is malformed. ``line`` is the 1-based line number."""
    17	
    18	    def __init__(self, line: int, reason: str):
    19	        super().__init__("line %d: %s" % (line, reason))
    20	        self.line = line
    21	        self.reason = reason
    22	
    23	
    24	@dataclass(frozen=True)
    25	class Entry:
    26	    date: date
    27	    category: str
    28	    amount: Decimal
    29	    note: str = ""
    30	
    31	
    32	def _parse_line(text: str, lineno: int) -> Entry:
    33	    stripped = text.strip(" \t\r\v\f")
    34	    parts = _WS_SPLIT.split(stripped, 3)
    35	    if len(parts) < 3:
    36	        raise ParseError(lineno, "expected DATE CATEGORY AMOUNT [NOTE]")
    37	    date_s, category, amount_s = parts[0], parts[1], parts[2]
    38	    note = parts[3].strip() if len(parts) > 3 else ""
    39	    if not _DATE_RE.match(date_s):
    40	        raise ParseError(lineno, "invalid date %r" % date_s)
    41	    try:
    42	        d = date(int(date_s[:4]), int(date_s[5:7]), int(date_s[8:10]))
    43	    except ValueError:
    44	        raise ParseError(lineno, "invalid date %r" % date_s) from None
    45	    if not _AMOUNT_RE.match(amount_s):
    46	        raise ParseError(lineno, "invalid amount %r" % amount_s)
    47	    return Entry(d, category.lower(), Decimal(amount_s), note)
    48	
    49	
    50	def parse(text: str) -> List[Entry]:
    51	    """Parse ledger text into entries, in file order."""
    52	    entries = []
    53	    for lineno, line in enumerate(text.splitlines(), 1):
    54	        s = line.strip()
    55	        if not s or s.startswith("#"):
    56	            continue
    57	        entries.append(_parse_line(line, lineno))
    58	    return entries
    59	
    60	
    61	def balance(entries: Iterable[Entry]) -> Decimal:
    62	    total = Decimal(0)
    63	    for e in entries:
    64	        total += e.amount
    65	    return total
    66	
    67	
    68	def by_category(entries: Iterable[Entry]) -> Dict[str, Decimal]:
    69	    out = {}  # type: Dict[str, Decimal]
    70	    for e in entries:
    71	        out[e.category] = out.get(e.category, Decimal(0)) + e.amount
    72	    return out
    73	
    74	
    75	def by_month(entries: Iterable[Entry]) -> Dict[str, Decimal]:
    76	    out = {}  # type: Dict[str, Decimal]
    77	    for e in entries:
    78	        key = "%04d-%02d" % (e.date.year, e.date.month)
    79	        out[key] = out.get(key, Decimal(0)) + e.amount
    80	    return out
    81	
    82	
    83	def filter_entries(
    84	    entries: Iterable[Entry],
    85	    category: Optional[str] = None,
    86	    since: Optional[date] = None,
    87	    until: Optional[date] = None,
    88	) -> List[Entry]:
    89	    cat = category.lower() if category is not None else None
    90	    out = []
    91	    for e in entries:
    92	        if cat is not None and e.category != cat:
    93	            continue
    94	        if since is not None and e.date < since:
    95	            continue
    96	        if until is not None and e.date > until:
    97	            continue

import pennywise as p
from decimal import Decimal
from datetime import date
def tp(text):

        r = p.parse(text); return repr(r)
    except p.ParseError as e:
        return "ParseError(line=%s, %r, isValueError=%s)" % (e.line, str(e), isinstance(e, ValueError))
    except Exception as e:
        return "OTHER %r" % e

    print("amount %r ->" % a, tp("2024-03-01 x %s" % a))

for big in ["9"*26, "9"*27, "9"*29]:

    except Exception as ex: print(len(big), "EXC", type(ex).__name__)
x = p.parse("2024-03-01 a 0.1\n"*3)

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in messages from the system in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork runs in the background and keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate. Subagents run in the background; you'll be notified when one completes. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).

description.description: A short (3-5 word) description of the task

prompt.description: The task for the agent to perform

subagent_type.description: The type of specialized agent to use for this task

model.description: Optional model override for this agent. Takes precedence over the agent definition's model frontmatter and the configured default subagent model. If omitted, uses the agent definition's model, else the default (inherits from the parent unless a default subagent model is configured). Ignored for subagent_type: "fork" — forks always inherit the parent model.

effort.description: Reasoning effort for this agent. Set this ONLY when the user, or instructions such as CLAUDE.md or a skill, explicitly ask that this agent or delegated work run at a specific effort level, never on your own judgment; otherwise omit it and the agent runs at its usual effort. Ignored for subagent_type: "fork": a fork runs at your own effort.

isolation.description: Isolation mode. "worktree" creates a temporary git worktree so the agent works on an isolated copy of the repo. "remote" launches the agent in a remote cloud environment (always runs in background; availability is gated).

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- `cd` carries to the next call only in the main session, if the command succeeds and ends inside the working directories. Outside them the shell returns to the start folder; otherwise it stays where it was. Prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. No `&` needed. You will be notified when it exits — do not poll its output file while waiting. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- GitHub notifies the owner of any `@name` written in a PR, issue, or comment. Write a bare `@name` only for a real login you mean to notify. Put roles, placeholders, and code (`@human`, `@reviewer`, `@types/node`) in backticks or drop the `@`, even when copied from project files.

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

tools.name: Read

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.

- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

Only use this when you genuinely need all of it or the user asked for the whole file; otherwise read it in parts with offset and limit, or search it.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).

I found three robustness bugs that print Python tracebacks and one spec deviation (mistyped `--since`/`--until` dates are accepted). Every brief behaviour and PRD acceptance criterion is otherwise met. The tests pass on Python 3.13 and 3.9.

`python3 -m venv` fails here because ensurepip is missing, so I used `python3 -m venv --without-pip /tmp/pw-rev/venv` and then `python3 -m pip --python /tmp/pw-rev/venv/bin/python install .`. That gave `import pennywise` from site-packages and a `pennywise` script that does `sys.exit(main())`. All probes ran against that installed script. I deleted the `build/` and `pennywise.egg-info/` that pip left in the repo, and no tracked files changed.

## (a) Acceptance criteria
| # | Criterion | Status | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `pip install .` gives the package and console script; Python ≥3.9; stdlib only | **Met** | Installed into the venv as above. `python3.9 -m unittest discover -s tests` → 66 OK. pyproject has `dependencies = []`. |
| 2 | `parse` fields, any spaces/tabs, note trimmed | **Met** | Tabs and runs of spaces work. `'\tnote  with   spaces \t '` → `'note  with   spaces'`. Types are date / lower str / Decimal / `""`. |
| 3 | Amount grammar | **Met** | `2500 +2500 2500.00 12 12.5 -0.99` accepted. `12.505 1,000.00 abc .5 12. -.5 1e3 NaN ١٢` rejected. |
| 4 | Blank/comment lines; ParseError | **Met** | Bad line after blank, comment and indented-comment lines → `line=6`. `2024-02-30` and `2023-02-29` rejected. ParseError is a ValueError, has `.line`, message `line N: …`. |
| 5 | balance / by_category / by_month / filter_entries | **Met** | `balance([])` is `Decimal('0')`. Month keys look like `2024-03`. `category="RENT"` matches; both date bounds inclusive; order kept. |
| 6 | `balance`, `--json` | **Met** | Prints `1557.50` and `{"balance": "1557.50"}`. The brief's `1457.50` is an arithmetic slip in the brief (2500 − 42.50 − 900 = 1557.50). |
| 7 | `summary`, `--by`, `--json` | **Met** | Output matches the brief. `--by month` works. `--by year` → exit 2. |
| 8 | `list` | **Met** | Format, stable sort, omitted note, `--json` all correct. `since > until` → empty, exit 0. |
| 9 | `add` | **Met** (one crash input, bug 1) | Creates the file. Adds a newline first if the file lacks one. Refusals leave the file byte-identical (sha256 checked) and don't create it. Notes with `\n`, `\r`, `\f` or U+2028 are refused. |
| 10 | `export` | **Met** | Header correct, `list` order, empty note → empty field. `--format json` → 2. `--json` → 2. |
| 11 | `-` reads stdin | **Met** | Works for balance, summary, list and export. |
| 12 | Exit codes | **Met** (except bugs 1–4) | No command, unknown command, bad `--by`/`--format`, `--since 2024-3-01`, `--since 2024-02-30`, missing file, directory and bad UTF-8 file all → 2 with empty stdout. Ledger errors → 1 with `pennywise: FILE: line N: …`. |
| 13 | Tests | **Met** | `python3 -m pytest -q` → 65 passed, 1 skipped, 53 subtests. The skipped pip-install test passes with `PENNYWISE_TEST_INSTALL=1`. |

## (b) Bugs / spec deviations

**Real bugs (traceback and wrong exit path)**
1. **`add` crashes when DATE starts with `#`** (`pennywise/cli.py:162-180`). `pennywise add h3.txt '#2024-03-01' food 5` prints a traceback ending in `IndexError: list index out of range` and exits 1. The built line looks like a comment, so `parse` returns `[]` and `entries[0]` fails. The file is not touched. Expected: exit 1 with `line 1: invalid date '#2024-03-01'`.
2. **Closed pipe prints a traceback** (`pennywise/cli.py:228`, no BrokenPipeError handling). These all exit 1 with `BrokenPipeError: [Errno 32] Broken pipe` on stderr:
   - `pennywise list big.txt | head -1`
   - `pennywise export big.txt | head -1`
   - `pennywise summary bigcat.txt | head -1` (20k categories)
   - `pennywise list - < big.txt | head -1`
   - `python -m pennywise list big.txt | head -1`

   Output smaller than the pipe buffer is unaffected (`list --json`, `balance`, a small `summary`).
3. **Amounts of 27+ integer digits crash** (`pennywise/core.py:103`). `quantize` needs more than the default 28-digit precision. Each of these gives a `decimal.InvalidOperation` traceback and exits 1:
   - `balance` of a line with amount `99999999999999999999999999999`
   - `99999999999999999999999999.99` plus `0.01`
   - `pennywise add huge3.txt 2024-03-01 food 99999999999999999999999999999` (file not created)

   The grammar accepts these amounts, so they should either format correctly or give a clean exit-1 error.

**Spec deviation**

4. **Mistyped `--since`/`--until` dates are accepted** (`pennywise/cli.py:26-32`). `int()` accepts signs and spaces, so `--since '+024-03-01'`, `'2024-+3-01'`, `'2024- 3-01'`, `'2024-03- 1'` and `'2024-03-+1'` all exit 0. `+024` even becomes year 24. Brief and PRD require exit 2 for a mistyped date and the `YYYY-MM-DD` format.

**Minor user-visible I/O findings (not criterion failures)**

5. **Non-UTF-8 stdin is accepted** (`cli.py:77`). Python's stdin uses `surrogateescape` here, so `pennywise list - < latin1.txt` exits 0 and echoes the raw `\xe9` byte (in list, json and export). The same file by path exits 2. Under `PYTHONIOENCODING=utf-8:strict` it correctly exits 2. This contradicts the PRD's "undecodable bytes → exit 2" for stdin.
6. **Line breaks inside a line shift line numbers** (`core.py:53`, `str.splitlines()`, as the PRD dictates). `\f`, `\v`, `\x1c`, U+0085, U+2028/2029 and a lone `\r` mid-line split the line:
   - `2024-03-01 food -5 a\fb` → `line 2: expected …` although the file has one line.
   - `note\f\nbad` → the error says `line 3` for the user's line 2. U+2028 behaves the same.
   - A stray `\r` in an LF file (`…abc\rdef\n<valid line>`) → `line 2` error.
   - Trailing `\f`/U+2028 at the end of an entry silently adds an empty "line", so every later line number is off by one.

   This conflicts with the brief's user-facing line counting.
7. **`add` cannot write a line that later misparses.** Every split character is refused in fields and inside the note. A trailing U+2028 is trimmed, and the printed line matches what was written. Not a bug, just confirming the probe.
8. **Argument parsing of values that start with `-`:**
   - Note `'-note'` → exit 2 "unrecognized arguments"; needs `--`.
   - Category `-food` → exit 2.
   - `--category -x` → exit 2; `--category=-x` works.
   - A note of literally `'--'` is silently taken as the separator and the entry is added with no note, exit 0. This silent data change is the worst of the four.
9. **A BOM is stripped only by the CLI.** `pennywise.parse("\ufeff2024…")` raises `invalid date '\ufeff2024-03-01'`. A double BOM fails in the CLI as well.
10. **Non-ASCII output on a non-UTF-8 stdout crashes.** `PYTHONIOENCODING=ascii pennywise list u.txt` gives a `UnicodeEncodeError` traceback, exit 1.
11. **Every uncaught exception exits 1**, the same code as "ledger mistake", and stdout is empty, so scripts can't tell crashes apart.
12. **Category is lower-cased with `lower()`, not `casefold()`.** `Straße` and `STRASSE` count as different categories. This is what the PRD specifies.
13. **`add` doesn't recognise a file ending in `\f` or U+2028 as ending a line** (`cli.py:189` only checks `\n`/`\r`). The new entry is glued onto the same visual line. Found by reading the code, not run.
14. **The packaging test leaves files in the repo.** Running it with `PENNYWISE_TEST_INSTALL=1` leaves `build/` and `pennywise.egg-info/` in the working tree. Both are gitignored.

## (c) Probe table (cmd = installed `pennywise`)
| Command | Observed | P/F |
|---|---|---|
| `add f.txt 2024-03-01 food -5` | `2024-03-01 food -5.00`, 0 | P |
| `add f.txt 2024-03-01 food -5 '-note'` | usage error, 2 | F (minor) |
| `add f.txt 2024-03-01 food -5 -- '-note'` | note `-note`, 0 | P |
| `add f.txt 2024-03-01 food -5 '--'` | added without a note, 0 | F (silent) |
| `add f.txt 2024-03-01 food -5 -- '--'` | note `--`, 0 | P |
| `add f.txt 2024-03-01 food -5 '-5'` / `'- dash note'` | added correctly, 0 | P |
| `add f.txt 2024-03-01 -food 5` | "required: AMOUNT", 2 | F (minor) |
| `add f.txt 2024-03-01 -- -food 5` | `-food 5.00`, 0 | P |

| `list f.txt --category=-x` | empty, 0 | P |
| `list - < f.txt`, `balance -`, `summary - --json`, `export -` | correct, 0 | P |
| `balance -x` | usage error, 2 | P |
| `list big.txt \| head -1` (20k lines) | BrokenPipe traceback, 1 | F |
| `export big.txt \| head -1` | BrokenPipe traceback, 1 | F |
| `summary bigcat.txt \| head -1` (20k groups) | BrokenPipe traceback, 1 | F |
| `summary big.txt \| head -1` (500 groups), `balance … \| head -1`, `list --json … \| head -1` | clean, 0 | P |
